title: 1 Chronicles 26:1–19
context: The divisions of the doorkeepers from the Korahite and Merarite families, including the large household of Obed-Edom, and the assignment of the temple gates and storehouse by lot.

verses.text: For the divisions of the doorkeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.
verses.arminianNotes: The divisions of the doorkeepers begin with the Korahites, Meshelemiah son of Kore. Arminian readers see guarding God’s house as genuine service, valued alongside music and sacrifice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s house protected by appointed servants. The phrase “of the sons of Asaph” here may refer to a different Asaph or a related line, and readers in this tradition hold the identification cautiously.

verses.text: Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth,
verses.arminianNotes: Meshelemiah’s sons are listed: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel. Arminian readers see family members trained together for faithful service at the gates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the passing of responsibilities through families. The careful naming honors those who served in less visible roles in God’s house.

verses.text: Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, and Eliehoenai the seventh.
verses.arminianNotes: Elam, Jehohanan, and Eliehoenai complete Meshelemiah’s seven sons. Arminian readers see a large family committed to the LORD’s service, each member counted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the record preserving each name. Readers in this tradition value the reminder that God sees and records the service of ordinary people.

verses.text: Obed-Edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sacar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth,
verses.arminianNotes: Obed-Edom’s sons are listed, from Shemaiah the firstborn to Nethanel the fifth. Arminian readers recall that Obed-Edom’s house was blessed when the ark stayed there in 2 Samuel 6:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s blessing on Obed-Edom’s household, as also noted in 1 Chronicles 13:14. Readers in this tradition hold the identification of this Obed-Edom with that earlier figure with some caution.

verses.text: Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peullethai the eighth; for God blessed him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ammiel, Issachar, and Peullethai complete eight sons, “for God blessed him.” Arminian readers see children received as God’s gift and dedicated to his service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator crediting God directly with Obed-Edom’s large family. The phrase underlines that household blessing comes from God rather than human effort.

verses.text: Sons were also born to Shemaiah his son, who ruled over the house of their father; for they were mighty men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Sons are born to Shemaiah, who ruled over their father’s house, “for they were mighty men of valor.” Arminian readers see strength and capability honored in God’s service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God equipping these men for their responsibilities. Guarding the temple required both character and strength, and the record notes both.

verses.text: The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed, and Elzabad, whose relatives were valiant men, Elihu, and Semachiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Shemaiah’s sons are named: Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, with valiant relatives Elihu and Semachiah. Arminian readers see a family known for courage and faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see valor passed through the generations. The list continues to emphasize capability, suiting the demanding role of the doorkeepers.

verses.text: All these were of the sons of Obed-Edom with their sons and their brothers, able men in strength for the service: sixty-two of Obed-Edom.
verses.arminianNotes: Obed-Edom’s descendants number sixty-two, “able men in strength for the service.” Arminian readers see a large, capable group devoted to guarding God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s blessing multiplied in the next generation. The number shows how one household’s faithfulness contributed significantly to temple service.

verses.text: Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, eighteen valiant men.
verses.arminianNotes: Meshelemiah has eighteen valiant sons and brothers. Arminian readers see another family contributing able men to the work of the gates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the record tallying each family’s contribution. Readers in this tradition see the Chronicler’s precision as honoring every group that served.

verses.text: Also Hosah, of the children of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, yet his father made him chief),
verses.arminianNotes: Hosah’s son Shimri is made chief, “though he was not the firstborn.” Arminian readers see responsibility given according to fitness, not merely birth order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a father’s appointment departing from the usual order. The text does not explain the reason, and readers in this tradition avoid supplying one.

verses.text: Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, and Zechariah the fourth. All the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen.
verses.arminianNotes: Hilkiah, Tebaliah, and Zechariah complete Hosah’s sons; all his sons and brothers number thirteen. Arminian readers see another family counted for service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful tally. The Merarite line of Hosah joins the Korahites, showing that service at the gates was shared among Levitical families.

verses.text: Of these were the divisions of the doorkeepers, even of the chief men, having offices like their brothers, to minister in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: These are the divisions of the doorkeepers, “having offices like their brothers, to minister in the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers see gatekeeping placed on equal footing with other ministries.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see all forms of service as ministry in God’s house. Readers in this tradition value the verse as a reminder that guarding and maintaining are part of worship.

verses.text: They cast lots, the small as well as the great, according to their fathers’ houses, for every gate.
verses.arminianNotes: “They cast lots, the small as well as the great, according to their fathers’ houses, for every gate.” Arminian readers see fairness in assigning the gates without favoritism.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lot used to receive God’s ordering, as with the musicians in 25:8. The repeated phrase about small and great stresses equal standing.

verses.text: The lot eastward fell to Shelemiah. Then for Zechariah his son, a wise counselor, they cast lots; and his lot came out northward.
verses.arminianNotes: The east lot falls to Shelemiah, and the north to his son Zechariah, “a wise counselor.” Arminian readers see wisdom recognized and valued among the gatekeepers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s assignment through the lot and the commendation of Zechariah’s wisdom. Shelemiah appears to be the Meshelemiah of verse 1, a variation readers note cautiously.

verses.text: To Obed-Edom southward; and to his sons the storehouse.
verses.arminianNotes: The south goes to Obed-Edom, and the storehouse to his sons. Arminian readers see responsibility for valuable stores entrusted to a household known for God’s blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the assignments made by lot. The storehouse required trustworthy guardians, and the record assigns it to Obed-Edom’s family.

verses.text: To Shuppim and Hosah westward, by the gate of Shallecheth, at the causeway that goes up, watchman opposite watchman.
verses.arminianNotes: Shuppim and Hosah receive the west, by the gate of Shallecheth, “watchman opposite watchman.” Arminian readers see careful coordination of guards around God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see orderly protection of the sanctuary. The exact locations named here are uncertain, and readers in this tradition do not press precise identifications.

verses.text: Eastward were six Levites, northward four a day, southward four a day, and for the storehouse two and two.
verses.arminianNotes: Six Levites serve eastward, four north, four south, and two and two at the storehouse. Arminian readers see practical planning for daily security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the detail of the arrangements. The numbers show that guarding God’s house was a steady, organized responsibility rather than an occasional task.

verses.text: For Parbar westward, four at the causeway, and two at Parbar.
verses.arminianNotes: At Parbar westward, four serve at the causeway and two at Parbar. Arminian readers see attention given even to smaller points of entry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see thoroughness in the arrangement. The meaning and location of Parbar are uncertain, and readers in this tradition hold any identification tentatively.

verses.text: These were the divisions of the doorkeepers; of the sons of the Korahites, and of the sons of Merari.
verses.arminianNotes: “These were the divisions of the doorkeepers; of the sons of the Korahites, and of the sons of Merari.” Arminian readers see the gatekeepers’ section summarized and completed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the closing summary confirming the families involved. The verse brings the doorkeepers’ list to an orderly conclusion before the treasurers.
